# COMMUNITY_INFLUENCE_AND_CONSENSUS_STRATEGY.md

> *Lid I-5 North is not primarily an engineering project. It is a civic project whose engineering serves a community vision.*

---

# Purpose

This document describes a strategy for building broad, durable public support for Lid I-5 North.

It is not public relations document. 

Its intended purpose is to build consensus around genuine community ownership so that, over time, the project becomes politically resilient, financially attractive, and socially indispensable.

The ultimate measure of success is that future elected and appointed officials view completion of Lid I-5 North as the obvious continuation of a community vision rather than the initiative of any particular organization or political leader.

---

# Guiding Principles

## 1. Lead with People, Not Infrastructure

Most transportation projects begin with engineering; successful civic projects begin with people and a vision that unites them.

People support projects that improve their lives—not projects that solve engineering problems.

Instead of discussing engineering:

- freeway lids
- ventilation
- bridge structures
- decking systems

let's begin with:

- children walking safely
- neighborhood connections
- local businesses
- parks
- public gathering
- cleaner air
- community identity

Engineering answers "How?"

AS A COMMUNITY we want to know "Why?"

---

## 2. Let's Imagine the Future, Not the Structure

The project is not a concrete lid with some grass and trees;
it is a vision for Seattle in 2080.

We need to ask repeatedly (the "5-whys"):

> What kind of city do we want our grandchildren to inherit?

This is a "root-cause" framing. It moves discussion away from short-term costs and engineering solutions and toward long-term investment and vision. 

---

## 3. Reconnection is our Core Story

The freeway divided neighborhoods.

The lid reconnects them.

Not simply physically, but:

- Socially.

- Economically.

- Environmentally.

- Emotionally.

Every communication from our team should reinforce this central narrative.

---

# The Story Framework - Our Narrative

Based on learning from RCI and other projects, nearly every successful civic project follows the same arc.

## Act 1 — The Place We Love

Celebrate what already exists.

Wallingford.

University District.

The Burke-Gilman Trail.

Lincoln High School.

Neighborhood businesses.

Street life.

Local history.

Indigenous history.

Community organizations.

The project begins with affection and pride-of-place.

---

## Act 2 — What Was Lost

Describe—not dramatize—the impacts of I-5.

Neighborhood fragmentation.

Lost streets.

Noise.

Pollution.

Reduced walkability.

Disconnected businesses.

Lost opportunity.

Avoid assigning blame.

History cannot be changed.

The future can.

---

## Act 3 — The Opportunity

Present the lid as civic repair.

Not restoration.

Not nostalgia.

An opportunity to build something better than either the freeway or the neighborhoods that preceded it.

---

## Act 4 — A Shared Future

Invite participation.

Residents become designers.

Businesses become partners.

Schools become contributors.

Artists become storytellers.

Children become ambassadors.

Everyone owns a piece of the future.

---

# Core Messages

## Instead of...

"We're covering I-5."

Say

"We're reconnecting Seattle."

---

Instead of

"We need a lid."

Say

"We have an opportunity to reconnect neighborhoods."

---

Instead of

"The freeway is the problem."

Say

"The freeway solved yesterday's problems.

Today Seattle has different needs."

---

Instead of

"This is expensive."

Say

"This is an investment that will serve Seattle for the next century."

# Build Ownership Before Design

Avoid presenting finished concepts too early.

Instead

Ask questions.

Examples

What would make you cross I-5 more often?

What businesses are missing?

Where should children play?

What makes Wallingford unique?

What makes the U District unique?

What should never be lost?

People support what they help create.

---

# Community Design Charrettes

Traditional public meetings often create opponents.

Design charrettes create collaborators.

Each session should produce drawings rather than opinions.

Suggested sequence

Session 1

Memory

What existed?

---

Session 2

Dreams

What should exist?

---

Session 3

Connections

Walking.

Cycling.

Transit.

Green space.

Business.

---

Session 4

Evaluation

Tradeoffs.

Priorities.

---

Session 5

Consensus

Preferred concepts.

---

# Visual Communication

People understand drawings faster than reports.

Prioritize

Historic photographs

Current aerial imagery

Before-and-after visualizations

Perspective sketches

Walking sequences

Short animations

Simple maps

Children's drawings

Watercolor concept sketches

Physical models

Avoid engineering drawings in early outreach.

# Measuring Success

Do not measure success only by engineering milestones.

Track

Public meeting attendance

Workshop participation

Volunteer hours

Business endorsements

Neighborhood endorsements

Letters of support

Student involvement

Media coverage

Social media sharing

Partner organizations

Grant interest

Private donations

Political endorsements

Repeat participation

The strongest indicator of success is repeated engagement.

---

# Strategic Narrative

Every successful civic project eventually becomes inevitable.

The purpose of outreach is therefore not persuasion alone.

It is to create a shared civic vision that many organizations independently champion.

When enough people begin telling the same story—

that Seattle can reconnect neighborhoods divided for half a century—

the project ceases to belong to any one committee.

It becomes Seattle's project.

That is the point at which engineering, funding, and politics become substantially easier.
